newsitem.title: USA: New CBOE chief sees resilience in options trade.
newsitem.headline: New CBOE chief sees resilience in options trade.

text.p: William Brodsky, chairman-designate of the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE), said equity options business was unlikely to see a repeat of the painful depression it experienced after the 1987 stock market crash.

Options trading volume has been maintained during the U.S. stock market's bull run in the past few years, but the rally has also raised concerns about a major correction in stock prices that could once again scare away investors from the potentially risky derivatives instruments.

Brodsky, currently president of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange who is due to take over the CBOE leadership from Alger "Duke" Chapman on February 24, said the market had become more mature since 1987.
"The potential diminution of volume should be much less because the use (of options) is so different," Brodsky said in an interview. He was in Tucson to attend a risk-management conference.
"The difference is, you saw a lot more speculative use of options by customers than you do now," he said.

He added that today's investors had a greater understanding of the more conservative ways to use options, such as buying puts to protect their stock holdings against a downturn or writing calls against their positions in a so-called "buy-write", or "covered call", trade.

In the latter strategy, investors use the premium income to enhance yields. The practice also can cushion the impact if the stock price drops and enhance gains if the stock makes minor advances, although the stock will be called away if it rallies sharply.
"In fact, one of my goals is to make sure people know they can use options against their investment at a time like this," Brodsky declared.

Although he said the exchange would put effort into fostering both institutional and retail business, he also looked for an expansion in the ranks of relatively experienced retail investors, notably the computer-literate younger generation.
He said his top priority was cultivating a broader base of investors through education and technological development.
"CBOE has done a very good job at that, but I think there's a tremendous potential audience out there. So a combination of education and marketing would be very important," he said.

On the technology front, Brodsky said focus was on two areas. On the trading floor level, he said the exchange aimed to further automate order flows by increasing the number of hand-held terminals to some 400 by the year-end from about 150 now. He said 70 percent of orders at CBOE were already coming in electronically, but he wanted to further reduce the use of paper and speed up turnaround of orders.

"The other side of this (technological development) is the use of computers for orders entered by customers through the Internet and otherwise," he added. "I think this is an area of tremendous growth...because I believe that there is a correlation between people who will use computers to enter orders and people who will be using options to fine-tune their equity portfolio."

He said the CBOE's website, http://www.cboe.com, had had some 700,000 inquiries a month in recent months. The growing interest has also been reflected in educational seminars run across the country by CBOE's Options Institute. All recent sessions have been packed, he said.

"The universe of customers and potential customers is so vast and, again, I believe there is a certain generational aspect to this," he said. "When you get used to dealing with the stock market, starting to understand equity options is a natural adjunct."
